steps.title: A river valley
steps.body: The Wachau is a narrow, 30 km stretch of the Danube valley in Lower Austria, about 80 km west of Vienna, between Melk and Krems. Vineyards climb steep, mostly south-facing slopes on stone terraces. It's small, about 1,300 hectares. Its landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000.

steps.title: Two climates meet
steps.body: The Wachau sits where cool air from the west, the Waldviertel forest, meets warm Pannonian air from the east. Cool nights from the forest keep acidity and aroma; warm days ripen the grapes. The Danube moderates temperatures. The result: ripe, powerful wines with fresh acidity.
steps.highlight: Cool forest air meets Pannonian warmth

steps.prompt: What gives the Wachau's wines both ripeness and freshness?
options: Warm Pannonian days and cool forest nights
steps.explanation: Two air masses meet over the valley.

steps.title: Terraces
steps.body: The terraces, held by dry-stone walls, were built over centuries, many by monks. They prevent erosion and create flat strips on slopes too steep to work otherwise. Soils on the terraces are primary rock, gneiss and granite, while lower slopes have loess. Maintaining them is costly; work is by hand.

steps.prompt: The Wachau's landscape is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

steps.title: What you learned
points: The Wachau is a 30 km stretch of the Danube
Cool forest nights meet warm Pannonian days
Steep stone terraces hold its vines
